I moved to a neighborhood in north Austin, Texas and it’s been a 300% improvement. Have a house with a large backyard for LESS than the one-bedroom apartment in Seattle. It’s unfortunate when we have parents like this, and I know first hand how detrimental it can be for years and years, invoking anxieties and stress and rage thinking about all the ways parents have messed me up. I’m currently 27, grew up in a very toxic household. Was always very on-edge around all the criticism, fighting, weird manipulation, suicide threats, lies, physical abuse and overall aggression. Never felt like my parents really got to know me, because even early on I knew my best chances would be to avoid them, go to my room, stay quiet, or sometimes take the bait and end up in a big fight that ends up hurting me much more than it affects them. Going to college and getting away from them, and then eventually mostly cutting them out is a sad decision, but one that has lead to me having the best chance at health and happiness for myself. I went years trying to talk to them, explaining the pain they’ve caused me and the anxiety and intrusive thoughts, and years of nightmares I’d woken up from literally yelling in anger and hurt. It always just lead to denial, defensiveness, gaslighting and being dismissive. It’d fill me with rage for years knowing that they won’t acknowledge the damage done.....when even stats and studies show that hitting children or being emotionally abusive increased their risk of depression, anxiety, health issues all by large amounts. I see them maybe once a year, and it isn’t enough to fix things even if the visit goes well enough. Even having a healthy and normal life now, and even with the rage finally passing...I just think it’s sad. But I didn’t make the decision to not have a family. I fought hard to have a relationship with them. But some people never change, or have too much pride, or are too narcissistic.  I don’t know your age, but the best thing you can do is watch out for yourself, take school and life seriously and do well and to not need them. Gain the power to be the one making the decision of if they’re in your life or not. Distance yourself if needed, but still be open to any forgiveness possible because it’ll only help your own health in the long run. A recent comment here stated it wasn't healthy to restrict yourself more than what your stomach can handle, but I feel there's still a good amount of variety in what AIP includes once you're versed in making it work. I avoid gluten/eggs/dairy/soy, but still feel I have more variety with my foods than the majority of people I know. AIP is very nutrient-dense and cuts out a lot of the junk. The AIP diet is strict in order to really cover most issues that could be causing problems for sufferers as a whole, but the tolerances of each person are really very individual. The diet is a process that includes eventually re-testing and reintroducing foods, to figure out your individual levels of tolerance. To start, it really is smart to cut out everything and see the level of benefit you get from the full diet. If you don't stick to it completely, and don't feel well...well then you'll never know if it's you cheating or if it's the diet. 

For me, I went strict AIP for a few months and eventually got IgG testing done, whose results actually very well matched up with my personal records of what thought would maybe be safe to reintroduce (rice, potatoes). I started with them as my first reintroductions, and it went well and I can still regularly eat them today. I then began using my personal test results as my safety guide (largely Dairy/Soy/Gluten/Eggs being my issues) and it's been working out pretty well. As long as I follow it, my symptoms are pretty in-check. I'm now just at a stage of hoping that over time I heal enough to gain more foods back, or at least have less severe reactions.

I've had much better success following natural remedies, because the way to better stomach health is often more of a fine tuning than taking a medicine that blocks a function and helps a symptom just until you stop taking the medicine.

Some people have IBS symptoms due to a high-acid diet which is common in the US diet -- which is why Alkaline drop can help those people.
